When "trying" is used as an adjective, it describes something — a situation, a person, an experience, or a period of time — that is difficult to deal with because it tests your patience, strength, or emotional endurance. It implies that something puts a real strain on you, wears you down, or pushes you to your limits.

Think of it this way: the adjective comes from an older sense of the verb "try," which once meant to test or to put to the test. So when something is "trying," it is essentially testing you — stretching your patience, energy, or ability to cope.

"Trying" is not just about something being hard. It carries a specific emotional and personal quality. It suggests that you are being strained — mentally, emotionally, or in terms of your patience. The difficulty is felt inside you, not just in the task itself.

This is what separates "trying" from the plain word "difficult":

  • A difficult math problem is hard to solve. It challenges your intellect.
  • A trying day is one that drains you — maybe things kept going wrong, people were uncooperative, or you had to hold yourself together under pressure.

You wouldn't naturally say "a trying math problem" — but you absolutely would say "a trying day," "a trying person," or "a trying situation." The word has a deeply human, emotional flavour to it.

Situations and experiences:
A situation that is stressful, frustrating, or hard to get through — especially one that demands a lot from you emotionally or mentally.

"It has been an incredibly trying week. I am completely exhausted."
"The long wait at the hospital was trying for the whole family."
"Getting through that difficult conversation was trying, but necessary."

Periods of time:
A stretch of time marked by hardship, stress, or suffering.

"These are trying times for many people around the world."
"The company went through a trying period after the financial collapse."

People:
A person who is trying is someone who tests your patience — perhaps they are demanding, frustrating, difficult to please, or exhausting to be around.

"He can be very trying sometimes — nothing ever seems to satisfy him."
"She is a kind woman, but her constant complaints make her rather trying to be around."
The Emotional Tone of the Word

"Trying" carries a tone of quiet suffering and endurance. When you use it, you are not saying something is impossible — you are saying it demands a lot from you and leaves you strained or worn out. It suggests that you are bearing through something, that it takes effort just to keep going.

It also carries a slightly dignified, restrained tone. Instead of saying "that was absolutely awful," a person might say "that was rather trying" — it conveys the hardship while remaining composed. This makes it a word that feels both expressive and measured at the same time.

"Trying" sits in the mid-to-upper range of difficulty and stress. It is stronger than "annoying" or "inconvenient," but it does not necessarily mean something catastrophic. It is a word for things that genuinely test your endurance — not a minor nuisance, but a real strain.

Taxing, demanding, gruelling, wearing, exhausting, draining, burdensome, stressful, frustrating, tough, hard to bear.

Each of these shares the idea of something that takes a toll on you, though "trying" specifically emphasises the sense of being tested and strained.
Easy, effortless, pleasant, enjoyable, comfortable, smooth, painless.
Register: When and Where Is It Used?

"Trying" (as an adjective) is a fairly formal and literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in written English, formal speech, or older literature than in casual everyday conversation. In everyday speech, people more often say "tough," "stressful," or "exhausting." However, "trying" is not rare — it is perfectly natural to use in conversation, especially when you want to sound thoughtful or restrained.

It is especially common in British English, though it is understood and used across all varieties of English.

If you want to remember this word in one sentence:

Something "trying" is something that tests and strains your patience, emotional strength, or endurance — making it hard to bear or get through.

Hold that idea, and you will always use this word correctly.
